items.definition: The main kinds of network, defined by size and purpose.
items.examples: A LAN in one office; a WAN linking offices nationally; a PAN of phone and earbuds.
items.examTip: LAN = one site; WAN = wide area; SAN = storage; PAN = personal.
keyFacts: LAN / WLAN covers one site, wired or wireless, so the organisation owns and controls it
WAN covers a large area, linking sites in different cities or countries
SAN is a network just for storage, and PAN links one person's devices nearby
The internet is the global WAN, so anything connected to it is exposed to attackers worldwide

items.definition: Networks restricted to particular users instead of the open internet.
items.examples: A staff intranet; an extranet for suppliers.
items.examTip: Intranet = staff only. Extranet = selected outsiders too.
keyFacts: Intranet is private and for staff only, so internal information isn't on the public internet
Extranet gives partners controlled access, so suppliers can use some systems without seeing everything
Cloud network provides private networking in the cloud, so systems can be added without new hardware

items.definition: Combining wired and wireless technology in one network, and the issues it raises.
items.examples: Wi-Fi access points connected to a wired backbone.
items.examTip: Issues: compatibility, admin (channels, IPs) and technical (signal, interference).
keyFacts: The 802 family of standards (e.g. 802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 Wi-Fi) lets wired and wireless kit work together
Protocols and access points must be compatible, or some devices can't connect
Admin of channels and IP addresses prevents clashes and interference between devices
Signal strength and interference affect wireless reliability, so access points must be placed carefully

items.definition: Diagrams showing how a network is laid out, sometimes with ports or addresses.
items.examples: Adding a firewall between the router and the switch.
items.examTip: Practise reading and changing diagrams, e.g. adding a firewall and labelling links.
keyFacts: Logical diagrams show how data flows, which helps plan security and troubleshoot
Physical diagrams show the real devices and cabling, so technicians can find equipment
May show ports or addresses, which helps configuration but should be kept confidential from attackers

items.definition: The qualities an organisation needs from its network, many linked to security.
items.examples: Designing for growth and to survive failures.
items.examTip: Security-related needs: security settings, reliability, fault tolerance, backups.
keyFacts: Scalability and performance, so the network copes as users and data grow
Reliability and fault tolerance, so one failure doesn't stop the whole network
Backup management and security settings, so data can be restored and the network is protected

items.definition: The physical and logical arrangement of devices on a network.
items.examples: A star network around a switch; a wireless mesh.
items.examTip: Physical = cable and device layout; logical = how data flows.
keyFacts: Physical topologies (star, extended star, hierarchical, mesh) decide how devices are cabled together
Logical topology (bus or ring) is how data actually travels, which can differ from the cabling
In a star, one broken cable doesn't stop the network, because each device has its own link

items.definition: How devices on a network share resources and responsibilities.
items.examples: Client/server with central control; peer-to-peer file sharing.
items.examTip: Client/server = central control and security; P2P = no server; thin client = processing on the server.
keyFacts: Peer-to-peer devices share directly, so it is cheap but hard to secure and back up centrally
Client/server gives central control, so security, accounts and backups are managed in one place
Thin client: the server does the processing, so data stays on the server and devices are cheap

items.definition: Running several virtual machines on one physical machine, isolating them from each other.
items.examples: Testing a suspicious program in an isolated virtual machine.
items.examTip: Security benefit: isolation contains threats and shrinks the attack surface.
keyFacts: Segments systems, so a problem in one virtual machine doesn't affect the others
Sandboxing and containers let suspicious software run safely in isolation
Smaller attack surface, because each service runs separately with only what it needs

items.definition: Security risks that come from relying on cloud services.
items.examples: Storage left open by default settings; hijacked accounts.
items.examTip: Risks: misconfiguration, reliance on the provider, insecure APIs, hijacking.
keyFacts: Wrong or default settings can leave data publicly exposed, e.g. open storage buckets
Reliance on the provider means an outage or breach at their end hits the organisation too
Insecure APIs give attackers a way into cloud data and services
Account hijacking gives an attacker full control of cloud resources, so MFA is essential

items.definition: Staff using their own devices for work, mixing personal and company data.
items.examples: Company email on a personal phone.
items.examTip: Issues: passwords, privacy, patching, wiping data when staff leave.
keyFacts: Company data on a private device can leak if the device is lost or shared with family
Enforcing password policy is harder on devices the organisation doesn't own
Keeping it patched depends on the owner, so devices may run with known flaws
Wiping company data when no longer needed (e.g. when staff leave) stops data leaving with them

items.definition: Other trends (SDN, SANs, IoT and remote working) and their security issues.
items.examples: A home worker needing a VPN on insecure home Wi-Fi.
items.examTip: Remote working risks: shared devices, home Wi-Fi, third-party tools. Needs a VPN.
keyFacts: SDN gives central management and segmentation, so the whole network can be controlled from one place
SAN needs redundancy, access control and encryption, because it holds the organisation's key data
IoT has default passwords and no patches, so devices can be hijacked into botnets
Remote working brings shared devices and home Wi-Fi, which are less secure than the office

items.definition: Devices people use directly, both mobile and fixed.
items.examples: Phones, laptops, tablets; servers, PCs, networked printers.
items.examTip: Split into mobile devices and fixed networked devices.
keyFacts: Mobile devices (phone, laptop, tablet, smartwatch) are easily lost, so they need encryption and remote wipe
Fixed devices (server, PC, printer, NAS) stay on site, so physical security protects them
Multifunction devices combine several functions, so one compromised device exposes several services

items.definition: Hardware that connects devices and networks and directs traffic.
items.examples: A switch in a LAN; a router joining networks.
items.examTip: Switch: connects devices in a LAN. Router: joins networks. Gateway: translates protocols.
keyFacts: Switch (managed or unmanaged) connects devices in a LAN; managed switches can be configured for security
Router and gateway connect different networks, deciding where traffic goes
Bridge, repeater and access point extend or join networks, including wireless access
Modem (DSL, fibre, wireless) connects the network to the internet provider

items.definition: The cables and wireless links that carry network data.
items.examples: Ethernet cable; fibre; Wi-Fi; Bluetooth.
items.examTip: Fibre is fast and hard to tap; wireless is easier to intercept.
keyFacts: Cable (Ethernet, USB) is hard to intercept without physical access, so it is more secure
Wireless (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, 5G) is convenient but signals can be picked up by attackers nearby
Fibre is very fast and hard to tap, and Li-Fi uses light, so it doesn't pass through walls

items.definition: The security risks of removable storage.
items.examples: A lost USB stick; an external drive spreading malware.
items.examTip: Risks: loss/theft, copying, malware, failure. Fix with encryption and secure disposal.
keyFacts: Loss, theft and copying are easy because media is small and portable
Can carry malware onto the network when plugged in
Media fails over time, so data on it can be lost
Encrypt and dispose of securely, so lost or thrown-away media can't be read

items.definition: The OSs, monitoring tools and applications running on a network.
items.examples: A packet sniffer; a log viewer; remote admin tools.
items.examTip: Monitoring tools help spot incidents: link to forensics.
keyFacts: Configured through a GUI, CLI or web interface, so admin access must be protected
Monitoring (performance, logs, vulnerability scans, packet sniffing) spots problems and attacks early
Remote working and document tools let staff collaborate, but must be secured

items.definition: The core set of rules for sending data across networks as packets.
items.examples: TCP splits a file into packets, IP addresses them, TLS secures the link.
items.examTip: Four-layer model; TLS adds security; error correction ensures delivery.
keyFacts: Four-layer model (application, transport, internet, link), so each layer handles one job
TLS gives secure connections, encrypting data such as HTTPS traffic
Packets with headers carry addresses, so each packet can find its own way to the destination
Error correction resends lost or damaged packets, so data arrives complete

items.definition: Ports identify services; packets are the chunks data is split into.
items.examples: Port 443 for HTTPS.
items.examTip: Packet = header (addresses), payload (data), trailer (error check). Know TCP vs UDP.
keyFacts: Hardware ports are physical sockets, while software ports are numbers that identify services, e.g. 443
Header, payload and trailer: addresses, the data itself, and an error check
TCP is reliable because it checks delivery; UDP is fast but gives no guarantee, so it suits streaming

items.definition: NAT maps private addresses to a public one; private IP ranges are reserved for internal use.
items.examples: Many home devices sharing one public IP.
items.examTip: Private ranges: 10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x. APIPA 169.254.x; loopback 127.0.0.1.
keyFacts: NAT types (static, dynamic, PAT) let many private devices share public addresses, which hides them
IPv4 is running out of addresses, so IPv6 provides vastly more
APIPA 169.254.x means DHCP failed, so the device can't reach the wider network
127.0.0.1 is the loopback address, used to test the device's own network software

items.definition: Dividing a network into segments to control access and limit an attacker's spread.
items.examples: Putting guest Wi-Fi on a separate segment from staff systems.
items.examTip: Benefits: limits access, stops lateral movement, smaller attack surface.
keyFacts: Limits access to devices and data, so users only reach their own segment
Stops attackers moving sideways from one compromised device to the rest of the network
Smaller attack surface, because each segment exposes less
Easier to contain damage, because an infected segment can be cut off

items.definition: Devices used to build and configure a network securely.
items.examples: A firewall filtering traffic; a router directing packets.
items.examTip: For "secure internet access" the expected answer is a FIREWALL.
keyFacts: Server, router and switch form the core, so they must be configured and locked down securely
Wireless access point lets devices join the network, so it needs strong encryption
Firewall, bridge and gateway control and join traffic between networks

items.definition: The service that turns domain names into IP addresses.
items.examples: www.example.com → its IP address.
items.examTip: DNS can be attacked by spoofing or poisoning.
keyFacts: Turns names into IP addresses (and back), so users can type names, not numbers
Results are cached, so lookups are faster, but a poisoned cache sends users to fake sites
Supports IPv6, so it works with the newer, larger address system

items.definition: Services that manage user identities and check them across a network.
items.examples: Active Directory accounts; single sign-on.
items.examTip: Types: single-factor, two-factor, multi-factor, SSO.
keyFacts: Active Directory and OpenLDAP store user accounts centrally, so access is managed in one place
Single-factor, 2FA, MFA and SSO, where SSO means one login gives access to many systems
Protocols PAP, CHAP and EAP: PAP sends passwords in plain text, so CHAP and EAP are more secure

items.definition: Automatically gives devices an IP address and network settings.
items.examples: A laptop joining Wi-Fi and getting its settings automatically.
items.examTip: DHCP has no built-in security, so a rogue DHCP server can be set up.
keyFacts: Assigns IP, gateway and lease automatically, so devices join the network without manual set-up
Config sets the address range, lease time and reservations, so key devices keep fixed addresses
No built-in security, so any device can request an address
Open to spoofing: a rogue DHCP server can send traffic through an attacker

items.definition: How traffic is routed between networks and how remote users connect securely.
items.examples: A VPN giving a home worker secure access.
items.examTip: A VPN is an encrypted tunnel, so intercepted data can't be read.
keyFacts: Static routing is set by hand and dynamic routing adapts automatically to changes and failures
BGP routes traffic across the internet between large networks
Remote access via VPN, so off-site users connect over an encrypted tunnel

items.definition: Shared file storage and shared printing across a network.
items.examples: A file server for shared documents; a print server queuing jobs.
items.examTip: File server = central storage; print server = manages shared printers.
keyFacts: File server gives central storage and sharing, so files are backed up and permissions controlled in one place
Print server queues and prioritises jobs, so many users can share printers
Manages printer drivers, so devices get the right driver automatically

items.definition: Web, email and real-time communication services, some without built-in encryption.
items.examples: A website over HTTPS; email via SMTP; a VoIP call.
items.examTip: SMTP and POP have no built-in encryption: a security weakness.
keyFacts: Web uses HTTP/HTTPS, and only HTTPS encrypts the traffic
Mail (SMTP, POP, MIME) is unencrypted by default, so emails can be read if intercepted
Email, VoIP, SMS and video calls all need securing, because they carry sensitive conversations
